title: Therac-25: treat interaction timing and hazard communication as design concerns
focus: A credible safety argument must account for temporal interactions, operator feedback, and what users are told when a defect is found.

sources.title: Leveson and Turner, An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, Part I
sources.limitations: Original investigators’ article, reprinted with permission from IEEE Computer 26(7), pp. 18–41. It explicitly notes uncertain details and the absence of a single official commission report.

sources.title: An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, Part III
sources.locator: Race-condition discussion; Government and user response
sources.limitations: Same article as Part I; one underlying publication. Regulatory descriptions are historical and are not current regulatory guidance.

facts.statement: The authors describe a race condition involving rapid edits and interacting software tasks, not simply an incorrect static input value.
They report that the FDA objected to an initial corrective notification because it failed to explain the defect, associated hazard, and urgency.

retrospective.boundary: Treatment prescription, software tasks, beam configuration, interlocks, operator display, patient feedback, manufacturer, and clinical users form the safety system.
interfaces: Operator editing → control state: valid individual actions can form an unsafe temporal sequence.
Manufacturer → clinical user: corrective instructions need a truthful hazard explanation and clear scope.

decision.question: What evidence supports a corrective release after a timing-dependent fault?
options: Patch the observed input sequence and send brief workaround instructions.
Reassess interacting states, independent protection, user feedback, and the complete corrective communication.
decision.recommendation: Require mechanism-focused tests and a bounded safety claim for the changed system.
decision.uncertainty: A reproduced software fault does not establish all contributing conditions or prove the resulting clinical system safe.

rows: Exercise edits at relevant state boundaries
Reproducible event traces and independent review
Identify safeguards independent of the faulty path
Explain hazard, affected configuration, action, and urgency
Readable instructions reviewed with representative users

questions: Why do static input tests miss temporal hazards?
What must a defect notice say beyond the workaround?
How would you communicate uncertain accident details without dismissing a credible safety signal?
answer_signals: Examines shared state, scheduling, and feedback.
Separates root-cause reproduction from overall safety acceptance.
Communicates hazard and uncertainty without minimizing either.
retrospective.transfer_exercise: Synthetic: a therapy-planning interface allows rapid mode edits while configuration is pending. Define a test plan and a hypothetical user notice; do not prescribe patient treatment.
retrospective.limits: No clinical advice, medical-device certification, or simulated radiation exposure is provided. The original authors’ uncertainty is retained.
